newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco ads curb lung-cancer news coverage - expert.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco ads curb lung-cancer news coverage - expert.

text.p: Cigarette advertising in leading women's magazines has contributed to the incorrect belief that breast cancer kills more women than lung cancer in America, a preventive medicine expert said Wednesday.

Testifying at a landmark secondhand-smoke trial, Dr. Thomas Houston said women's magazines were the top source of health information for women but Redbook, Cosmopolitan and others steered away from lung cancer stories so as not to upset cigarette manufacturers who buy advertising.
"More women get breast cancer but more women die from lung cancer," said Houston, head of the American Medical Association's anti-tobacco campaign and preventive medicine section.

Houston said women's magazines run more stories on breast cancer and sexually transmitted diseases such as AIDS due "to the effect of cigarette advertising dollars on the coverage of lung cancer and other cigarette-related diseases."

Lawyers defending seven cigarette makers and two trade groups in the secondhand-smoke case fiercely and repeatedly challenged Houston's testimony and secured the right to question the physician without the jury in the courtroom.

"Tobacco advertising has a censoring effect," Houston said with the jury absent. He also said a journalism contest that he oversees for health stories on tobacco-related topics published in magazines with cigarette advertising had not had a single entry since 1995.

Trial Judge Robert Kaye, who had earlier forbidden the plaintiffs lawyer from questioning Houston about some tobacco-industry papers, agreed with the tobacco lawyers that much of Houston's testimony should not be allowed and cut off the questions on advertising.

The latest in a string of experts to testify on behalf of some 60,000 non-smoking airline flight attendants claiming injuries from secondhand smoke, Houston also said the tobacco industry had for decades campaigned against serious medical research into the dangers of smoking and lobbied for continued acceptance of smoking in restaurants and other public places.

Tobacco industry officials have argued that general health, genetic disposition and other factors were possible causes of lung cancer among smokers when no mainstream researcher or physician believed so, Houston said.

Houston said the AMA, the main organisation for U.S. doctors with some 300,000 members, has formally advised researchers and hospitals to refuse research money from tobacco companies and tobacco groups such as the Council for Tobacco Research-USA on the ground that they "do not, in some instances, conform to legitimate scientific principles."
The Council for Tobacco Research is a defendant in the secondhand-smoke trial and funds biomedical research, much of in it partnership with other organisations.
The physician also said that smokers overwhelmingly pick up their first cigarettes as teenagers, at an age when the full health risks of smoking are seldom understood,

"The choice to smoke is made by people who are 14 ... not basically by people who are 30 or 40. Most people who smoke began when they were children, before they had a full understanding of their choice," Houston said.

Now in its second week of testimony, the trial is the first to test a claim of injuries from secondhand smoke. Lawyers pressing the case for flight attendants say they were hurt by passengers smoking aboard U.S. airliners and have said they will seek $5 billion or more in damages.

The plaintiffs claim the tobacco industry sold a dangerous product and hid its dangers, while the tobacco defendants say secondhand smoke is not a substantial health risk and that the flight attendants exposure to secondhand smoke was trivial.
